title: Manifesting the Presence of the Lord
excerpt: Pst. Kiseku Muange’s Semester Premier message challenged students to pursue God’s presence, discover their assignment, build people, develop their gifts, and remain faithful beyond the excitement of a new beginning.
content:
“If Your Presence does not go with us, do not bring us up from here.” — Exodus 33:15

Our Semester Premier Sunday Service was marked by worship, teaching, reflection and a strong challenge to both continuing students and the freshers beginning their journey at Mount Kenya University.

Ministering on “Manifesting the Presence of the Lord,” Pst. Kiseku Muange began from the encounter between Moses and God in Exodus 33:12–15.

Moses had received an assignment, but he understood that an assignment from God could not be fulfilled independently of God. He needed God's presence, God's direction and people who could walk with him.

From this foundation, Pst. Kiseku presented several principles necessary for a believer who desires not only to experience God's presence, but to carry that presence into their assignment.

The Foundations: Vision, Grace and People

Three foundations emerged early in the message:

1. Vision — know your assignment.

Drawing from Proverbs 29:18, the congregation was challenged to seek clarity concerning what God has placed before them. Vision gives direction. Without it, distraction easily takes over.

2. Grace — you need God for what He has called you to do.

An assignment may be clear, but human ability alone is insufficient. God's grace enables a person to carry what He has entrusted to them.

3. People — you cannot do it alone.

Moses understood that he needed people. Throughout the sermon, this principle resurfaced through mentorship, accountability, partnership, leadership and submission.

The message was therefore not simply “discover your vision.” It was:

Receive the vision, depend on God's grace, and allow the right people to help you carry it.

Four Tools for Manifesting His Presence

The sermon then developed into practical tools for walking in and manifesting God's presence.

1. A Deep Desire for Him

The first was desire.

From Psalm 37:4, Pst. Kiseku emphasized that there must be genuine delight in God before His presence becomes something we continually pursue.

This desire is accompanied by joy. Zechariah 10:7 speaks of hearts rejoicing in the Lord, while Nehemiah 8:10 reminds us that:

“The joy of the Lord is your strength.”

The Christian walk cannot survive indefinitely as an obligation. There must be a heart that genuinely desires God.

2. A Deep Conviction of Him Who Sent You

The second tool was conviction.

In Luke 1:19, Gabriel declares that he stands in the presence of God and was sent by Him.

Gabriel knew where he stood, who had sent him and why he had come.

In the same way, a believer should develop conviction concerning their assignment. Whether one's future lies in ministry, medicine, business, media, entrepreneurship, leadership or another sphere, there should eventually be clarity about what one is building and why.

3. A Desire to Fulfil the Mandate

The third emphasis was mandate.

Pst. Kiseku challenged students to ask themselves:

Why am I here? What has God entrusted to me? What should be different about me five years from now?

One memorable statement summarized this:

“Your light is in the direction of your assignment.”

University therefore should not merely become a cycle of classes, examinations and social activities. It can also become a place for discovering purpose, developing gifts, learning skills and preparing for what lies beyond campus.

4. Meekness, Humility and Dependence on God

The fourth tool centred on meekness—recognizing that we cannot accomplish God's assignment independently of Him.

Several Scriptures were given for personal study:

Psalm 37:11 • Exodus 33:15 • Matthew 5:5 • Numbers 12:3

Moses was particularly significant here. Despite the magnitude of his assignment, he understood his dependence upon God's presence.

The lesson was simple: there is no genuine manifestation that makes humility unnecessary.

“Will I Still Find You?”

The message then became particularly personal for the freshers.

Pst. Kiseku repeatedly asked:

“Will I still find you?”

Will I still find you serving?

Will I still find you praying?

Will I still find you worshipping?

Will I still find you attending ministry practices?

Will I still find you committed months from now?

The question was anchored in Acts 6:4:

“But we will give ourselves continually to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”

The emphasis was on continually.

Beginning is important, but remaining is harder.

The excitement of joining university eventually settles. The excitement of joining a ministry can fade. New friendships become ordinary. Responsibilities increase.

What remains after the excitement disappears reveals the depth of our commitment.

The challenge to the freshers was therefore not merely to attend church, but to stay long enough to grow.

Beyond the Sermon: A Charge to Build

From the central teaching on God's presence, the message broadened into a practical charge about leadership, skills, business, relationships and building people.

This was where Pst. Kiseku drew extensively from his own journey and experiences.

One word repeatedly captured this part of the message:

“Build. Build. Build.”

Build People, Not Titles

Current leaders were challenged not to measure their service merely by the offices they have occupied.

At the end of a leadership season, saying “I was a worship leader,” “I was an usher,” “I was an executive,” or “I chaired a ministry” is not enough.

A more difficult question is:

Who did you build?

Who became better because you served?

Who did you teach?

Who did you disciple?

Who can continue after you leave?

This is particularly important within a university Christian Union because leadership constantly transitions.

Today's fresher may be tomorrow's ministry leader.

Today's ministry member may become tomorrow's chairperson.

The responsibility of current leaders is therefore not merely to run today's church successfully, but to prepare tomorrow's church intentionally.

Pst. Kiseku summarized the principle in one of the strongest statements of the service:

“The church of God is built when principles are understood, protocols are not undermined, and the presence of God is highly guarded.”

Association, Mentorship and Accountability

Another major theme was the importance of the people around us.

Pst. Kiseku challenged students not to become envious when they encounter somebody who is better than them.

There will always be someone who sings better, leads better, understands Scripture better, communicates better or possesses a skill we have not yet developed.

Instead of competing with such people, learn from them.

The relationship between Elijah and Elisha was used to illustrate the value of walking with someone who carries what you desire to develop.

The same principle appears in Proverbs 13:20:

“He who walks with wise men will be wise...”

At the same time, 1 Corinthians 15:33 warns that bad company corrupts good character.

The people around us therefore matter.

Some relationships reinforce our assignment; others gradually pull us away from it.

And alongside association comes accountability. Gifts, ambitions and calling should not become excuses for isolation.

One of the memorable principles from this part of the message was:

“You cannot be a master if you are not mastered.”

Learn to be led before demanding to lead.

Learn to receive correction.

Learn to honour.

Learn from people who have gone ahead.

Preparation Before Manifestation

The congregation was also challenged about the importance of testing and preparation.

A product should be tested before distribution. A gift should be developed before demanding a platform. A leader should have evidence of faithful stewardship.

Pst. Kiseku put it this way:

“Don't be quick to manifest that which you lack a blueprint of.”

David was used as an illustration. Before standing publicly before Goliath, there was already a private history behind him.

There was a track record.

That principle applies beyond ministry.

Before expansion comes preparation.

Before influence comes substance.

Before distribution comes development.

Before public manifestation comes private building.

The challenge was therefore to stop being obsessed only with being seen and begin becoming serious about being built.

Possess. Multiply. Supply. Distribute.

Business and entrepreneurship formed an important practical application of the sermon.

Pst. Kiseku presented a progression for building something successfully:

Possess → Multiply → Supply → Distribute

First, understand and possess what has been placed in your hands.

Then develop and multiply it.

Build enough capacity to supply.

Only then pursue wider distribution.

The lesson was that trying to distribute something that has never been sufficiently developed eventually drains the person carrying it.

Students interested in business were therefore encouraged not merely to dream about companies and brands, but to develop products, skills, systems, partnerships and capacity.

And importantly, they were reminded that being serious about God does not prevent someone from becoming excellent in business or professional life.

Faith and Skill Belong Together

The message also challenged the idea that spirituality eliminates the need for competence.

If you are interested in multimedia, learn multimedia.

If you are a worshipper, develop your gift.

If you are an instrumentalist, practise.

If you are an usher, understand protocol.

If you want to build a business, understand your product and market.

Prayer does not remove the responsibility to develop skill.

Instead, God's presence should give purpose and direction to what we are developing.

The Christian Union itself provides opportunities for students to serve while sharpening abilities that may become valuable far beyond campus.

A Special Word to the Freshers

Much of the practical counsel eventually returned to the first-year students.

The message was straightforward:

Do not waste your campus years.

University gives enormous freedom. With that freedom comes the ability to choose relationships, environments, habits and priorities that can either build or diminish the future.

From 1 Timothy 4:12, the freshers were reminded:

“Let no one despise your youth...”

Being young does not make your contribution insignificant.

Start learning now.

Start serving now.

Start developing your skill now.

Start becoming disciplined now.

Find mentors.

Join a ministry.

Build healthy relationships.

Study.

Pray.

Discover what you carry.

And become intentional about the person you want to be when your university years are over.

The encouragement eventually became a declaration:

“You are meant for nations.”

But greatness requires preparation.

Scriptures to Revisit After the Service

The sermon contained several passages worth returning to during personal study:

  • Exodus 33:12–15 — Moses, God's presence and the assignment
  • Proverbs 29:18 — the importance of vision
  • Acts 6:1–4 — continual devotion to prayer and the Word
  • Psalm 37:4 — delight and desire for God
  • Psalm 37:11 — meekness
  • Zechariah 10:7 — joy in the Lord
  • Nehemiah 8:10 — the joy of the Lord as strength
  • Luke 1:19 — conviction concerning the One who sends
  • Matthew 5:5 — blessed are the meek
  • Numbers 12:3 — the meekness of Moses
  • Proverbs 13:20 — walking with the wise
  • 1 Corinthians 15:33 — the influence of association
  • 1 Timothy 4:12 — refusing to despise youth
  • Malachi 3:10 — the principle of testing
  • Philippians 4:19 — God's provision

These passages capture the major threads running through the message: presence, vision, consistency, humility, association, preparation, purpose and trust in God.

From the Word to Prayer

The service concluded by moving from teaching into prayer.

After speaking directly to students carrying ideas for businesses, brands and future enterprises, Pst. Kiseku invited those desiring to venture into business forward for prayer.

The congregation stretched out their hands as prayer was made over business ideas, partnerships, direction and the assignments represented at the altar.

It brought the message back to where it began.

Moses had an assignment, but he did not want to move without God's presence.

Likewise, we may carry ambitions for ministry, careers, businesses, leadership and influence—but the challenge of the Semester Premier Sunday Service was not merely to go.

It was to know Who goes with us.

And perhaps that is the message worth carrying into the semester:

Know your assignment. Stay in His presence. Build yourself. Build people. Honour the process. Develop what God has placed in your hands—and remain faithful enough to leave something behind that can continue after you.
